content.p: The Hells Angels are the most recognisable motorcycle club in the world and, to police in several countries, one of its most persistent criminal organisations. Started in California in 1948, the club grew from a scatter of local groups into a network that US authorities say operates on six continents. Its members have been celebrated in books and films, blamed for a killing in front of a rock band's audience, and convicted in federal courts of racketeering, murder conspiracy and drug trafficking.

The club's own answer has long been that it is a club and nothing more. CBC News noted in 2009 that the organisation "denies it's anything more than a motorcycle club". The man who did most to build it, Sonny Barger, put the argument in blunter terms in a 2000 interview quoted by NPR: "They say we're organized crime, but if you took every Hells Angel on the face of the Earth and got rid of them you wouldn't drop the crime rate in the world one-tenth of one percent."

Prosecutors describe the group differently, and the court record since 2017 gives their case unusual detail. This account follows the club from its early years in California through its two best-known episodes of violence, Altamont and the Quebec biker war, to recent federal trials. Only convictions and verdicts are stated as fact; everything else is attributed.
content.h2: From California clubs to one brotherhood
content.p: CBC News and the US National Gang Intelligence Center date the club to 1948 in California. Its character was shaped less by that first founding than by the Oakland chapter, which Sonny Barger started in 1957. According to Sky HISTORY, Barger was a teenager who had left the Army after officials found he had lied about his age. He had joined the Oakland Panthers motorcycle club the year before but found no real brotherhood there, and he formed the Angels chapter with a group of veterans he drank with.

NPR reported that Barger soon learned that other Hells Angels clubs existed in California and helped to unify them. Sky HISTORY says he took over leadership of the San Bernardino chapter in 1958 when its president was jailed, and then introduced hierarchies and rules that framed membership as a lifelong commitment, enforced by punishment. The same account says he also tried to soften the club's image with charity work.

The outside world met the Angels in the 1960s. Sky HISTORY records that in 1965 members turned up at a Berkeley rally against the Vietnam War, intending to confront protesters they judged unpatriotic rather than to join them. Violence escalated quickly. Rolling Stone says the club was already heavily involved in drug trafficking and infamous for clashes with police and with anti-war protesters, whom Barger called "peace creeps".

Rolling Stone says the club gained prominence in 1967 with the publication of a book. The writer Hunter S. Thompson lived among the bikers for about a year, according to Rolling Stone, and published "Hell's Angels: The Strange and Terrible Saga of the Outlaw Motorcycle Gangs", with Barger as its central figure. Rolling Stone dates the book to 1967 and NPR calls it a 1966 exposé. Barger later told Rolling Stone that Thompson "made us even more of a myth than we were at the time", and that Thompson never tried to act like one of them. Thompson, quoted by NPR, described Barger as "clearly the most competent person around".

On 6 December 1969 the Hells Angels were at the Altamont Speedway in Livermore, California, for a free concert headlined by the Rolling Stones. NPR describes them as bikers hired as security staff; Rolling Stone calls them unofficial security. During the Stones' performance, Meredith Hunter, an 18-year-old audience member according to Sky HISTORY, was stabbed to death by a member of the club. A film crew shooting the documentary "Gimme Shelter" captured the stabbing.

The club's account, as relayed by Barger, was that Hunter had pulled a gun on one of its members. NPR reports that Barger argued the Angels acted in self-defence, and that the member who was charged was acquitted. Barger blamed the crowd for the escalation: "when they started kickin' our bikes, man, that started it", he said, quoted by Rolling Stone. He added: "Mick Jagger used us for dupes, man."

Sky HISTORY says the violence began after festival-goers allegedly interfered with members' motorcycles, and that fights broke out. Rolling Stone writes that the club's cultural appeal was short-lived after Altamont.

The legal pressure that followed fell especially on Barger. Rolling Stone lists charges against him ranging from drug-running to kidnapping to attempted murder, most of which did not send him to prison. In 1973 he was convicted on a narcotics charge and received a sentence of nearly five years. NPR counted about 13 years served in various prisons in total, according to news reports.

His most favourable outcome came in 1980, when he was acquitted on a racketeering count and a mistrial was declared on a charge of conspiracy to violate the racketeering law, according to NPR. Barger called it one of his most satisfying experiences. In 1988, according to NPR, a jury convicted him on a conspiracy count under federal firearms and explosives law; NPR says the plots were aimed at members of a rival gang. He received six years and was released in 1992. Rolling Stone dates the arrest in that case to 1987, when he and 13 other members faced narcotics, weapons, conspiracy and explosives charges.

Barger kept his place in the club and his public profile. He wrote a best-selling autobiography, "Hell's Angel", and appeared as an actor in "Sons of Anarchy". He died at home in Livermore on 29 June 2022 of liver cancer, according to his former attorney Fritz Clapp, who spoke to the Associated Press. He had asked that a note be posted after his death; it said in part: "Keep your head up high, stay loyal, remain free, and always value honor." Sky HISTORY reports that more than 7,000 people attended his funeral.

The club's expansion was not only American. According to Vice, the Hells Angels crossed the border on 5 December 1977, when the Popeyes, a Quebec gang, joined them at a party in Laval. The Ontario Provincial Police staff sergeant Len Isnor told Vice the Angels had chosen the Popeyes because of their reputation for prosperity and violence, and because of access to the Port of Montreal. CBC describes the Montreal chapter as the largest and most feared in Canada.

Vice reports that from 1977 to 1982 the Angels fought the Outlaws, a rival club from Ontario, in what became known as the First Biker War. In March 1985, Vice says, five members of the Laval chapter were lured to a meeting in Lennoxville, Quebec, and murdered, with a sixth member killed a couple of weeks later. Vice presents this as an act of internal discipline meant to show that a more business-like management had taken over. Vice does not say who was convicted of the killings; it says that by many accounts the murders laid the seeds of the later war.

Vice traces the later war to a split. Salvatore Cazzetta, who had belonged to a club that the Angels were courting, was reportedly angered by the killings and, with his brother Giovanni, founded the Rock Machine. CBC dates the group's emergence to 1986. The two sides coexisted for a time. In 1994, Vice reports, with the Rock Machine leaderless after Cazzetta's arrest on drug smuggling charges, the Angels moved to take over street-level distribution and the clubs went to war.

The death toll varies by source. CBC says the conflict claimed more than 150 lives, among them two prison guards and 11-year-old Daniel Desrochers, killed when a car bomb exploded outside a biker hangout. Vice gives about 160 deaths by 2002, when the war ended with the Angels dominant. The boy's death and the public outrage prompted Bill C-95, passed in 1997, which raised penalties for offenders shown to belong to established criminal organisations.

The aftermath produced two large police operations. Early in 2009 a man named Gérald Gallant, who had confessed to carrying out contract killings during the war, assisted police in arresting 11 people accused of ordering or committing murders in it. CBC adds that he pleaded guilty to 27 slayings across three decades. In April 2009, CBC reports, police targeted more than 150 people linked to the Angels in raids, mostly in Quebec. Vice separately describes Operation SharQc, a 2009 sweep, as producing 156 arrests, and says many charges were thrown out when the mega-trial was judged to have violated defendants' charter right to a speedy trial.

The Angels also spread westward. Vice reports that on 29 December 2000 almost 200 Ontario bikers patched over to the club, while the Rock Machine joined the Bandidos on 1 December. CBC says within a year the Angels had taken in members of Satan's Choice, Last Chance and the Para-Dice Riders, a move that gave them at least 100 members in the Toronto area, which it called the highest concentration of Hells Angels in the world. In 2009, CBC reported, the Criminal Intelligence Service Canada estimated 34 chapters and about 460 full members nationwide and described the club as the country's largest outlaw motorcycle gang. A 2004 CISC report, CBC says, found it relied primarily on drug trafficking for income.

The most detailed recent look inside the club's workings comes from a federal racketeering prosecution in San Francisco. On 10 October 2017 a grand jury indicted eleven members and associates of the Sonoma County charter (HASC). The charges included murder, conspiracy to commit murder, narcotics distribution, assault, robbery, extortion, firearms offences, obstruction of justice and witness intimidation. In the indictment's words, the Hells Angels are a violent transnational outlaw motorcycle gang.

The first trial, in 2022, centred on the murder of Joel Silva, a former member of the Sonoma charter. A jury convicted Jonathan Nelson, Brian Wayne Wendt and Russell Taylor Ott, each of whom the Justice Department said played a role in the killing on 15 July 2014. KRON4 reported that they were sentenced to life in prison. According to the indictment quoted by KRON4, Nelson, then the Sonoma president, arranged for Ott to take Silva to Fresno, where Wendt, the Fresno charter's president, shot him in the back of the head at the clubhouse. His body was incinerated the next morning, prosecutors said.

The second trial lasted two months before US District Judge Edward Chen and ended in May 2023. Prosecutors said that at a motorcycle event in Laconia, New Hampshire, Silva had threatened a member of the Salem, Massachusetts, charter, which Ranieri, Wendt and Nelson regarded as disrespectful, and that the three agreed he had to be killed. The jury convicted Christopher Ranieri, president of the Salem charter, of racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to commit murder in aid of racketeering. Raymond Foakes, a former Sonoma president, was convicted of racketeering conspiracy, assault with a dangerous weapon in aid of racketeering, and witness intimidation. The assault was a multi-hour beating of a former member by Foakes and others to expel him from the club. One more defendant in that trial, Brian Burke, was cleared of a single witness-intimidation count.

By then nine of the eleven defendants had been convicted, one of whom had died, the Justice Department said. They included five former presidents of three charters. Five defendants pleaded guilty to racketeering conspiracy and received prison terms of up to 84 months, according to KRON4. FBI Special Agent in Charge Robert Tripp said the prosecution "brings an end to that fear". The statutory maximums were life for Ranieri and 60 years for Foakes; the pages consulted do not give their sentences.
content.h2: A Romanian chapter and the reach abroad
content.p: The same racketeering law has been used against members outside the United States. Marius Lazar, a Romanian national who founded the club's Romanian chapter, was convicted by a federal jury in Beaumont, Texas, on 17 November 2023. On 15 January 2025 he received 300 months in federal prison. The counts were racketeering conspiracy, a conspiracy to import cocaine and a money-laundering conspiracy.

According to the court documents and trial evidence summarised by Homeland Security Investigations, Lazar joined a conspiracy through a member from New Zealand to buy more than 400 kilograms of cocaine from a person he believed was a powerful trafficker, but who was an undercover US officer. Lazar also asked the officer to have two members of a rival Romanian club killed and offered rifles, grenades and armoured vehicles. Conspirators sent nearly $1 million, by bank wire and Bitcoin, as payment. Two co-defendants remained fugitives.

The US government said the club is active on six continents. CBC, in 2009, cited the US National Gang Intelligence Center as counting more than 2,000 members in the United States and 26 other countries.
